newsitem.title: UK: New EMU tensions spell trouble for frazzled bonds.
newsitem.headline: New EMU tensions spell trouble for frazzled bonds.

text.p: European bond markets face a long, troubled summer amid deepening gloom about the start of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said on Monday.
At best, markets will start to price in a wider group of countries in EMU, and therefore a softer euro. At worst, they will start to price in a delay.
The confusion will leave already fragile markets ripe for sharp moves and peripheral markets like Italy and Spain particularly vulnerable, analysts said.

"Last week it was more probable there would be a softer EMU," said Ricardo Antoniol, economist at Bank of America in Milan. "Now after the discussion between the Bundesbank and Waigel about the gold issue this does not seem so clear."
"On one side, we have the positive effect of the spread narrowing on the other hand the interest rates in Germany and France are going to rise," he said.

European futures markets opened weaker on Monday as they wrestled with the left's victory in French elections and the continuing row in Germany over Bonn's plans to revalue Bundesbank gold and currency reserves.

French and Italian markets showed the biggest losses. By 0939 GMT, June notionnel futures were quoted at 128.14, down 36 basis points from Friday. Italian BTP futures were down 59 basis points at 128.31.

In the cash market, 10-year French bonds were yielding only seven basis points below 10-year Bunds, compared with 12 basis points on Friday. Italian bonds trailed Bunds by three basis points from Friday.
Questions remained over France's future commitment to getting into fiscal shape for EMU but the Socialist's overall strategy was quickly spelled out by the Party's spokesman.

"We all stand to gain if Italy and Spain are in monetary union, if there is a political government alongside the European Central Bank, if Europe no longer means austerity," Party spokesman Francois Hollande said in a radio interview.
Meanwhile Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition vowed to push ahead with its gold revaluation plans, despite objections from the Bundesbank.
On Sunday, Hans Tietmeyer, the head of the Bundesbank, denied a report in Der Spiegel magazine that he had proposed a delay in EMU's 1999 start date.
The information noise left markets groping for a footing.
"For the moment the best guess is a wider EMU with a more flexible interpretation of criteria," Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London said.
"The bottom line from Germany and France is that there is probably no more fiscal tightening to come through of any significance," he said.
In that context, Goldman was negative on all European bond markets and saw limited scope for further convergence of some of the peripheral markets, Bevan said.

"Of the relatively high-yielding markets, the ones we would prefer are the ones that are sheltered from EMU turbulence -- UK, Denmark and Sweden," he said. "It means basically downgrading Europe in a global context."
Antoniol at Bank of America forecast the BTP/Bund spread to swell out to 190 basis points on a three-month view. Italian economics did not support such a narrow spread, he said.
John McNeill, bond strategist at I.D.E.A. in London, said market turmoil would likely increase when Germany begins to respond to the French Socialists' EMU vision.
"When that rhetoric starts to hit the wire that's going to be messy, for Italy in particular," he said.
Longer term however, he expected the dust to settle as the EMU process overcomes these short-term hurdles.

"The vast majority of governments in Europe are now pink (politically) so the consensus in Europe is building towards placing more emphasis in the euro zone on things like generating employment," McNeill said.
"If that takes a slightly weaker currency, so be it," he added. --International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
